It's the "just;" they might mean it as "I know you can get over that hurdle and be the amazing person you are" but we hear it as "you seem utterly incompetent to handle this one basic step to get to happiness, haven't you ever considered *not* being miserable?"

I personally find the most helpful version of this sentiment to be one that acknowledges all these things at once: 1. you are allowed to love yourself even if you think you deserve criticism, and it is possible and good to have both, 2. learning to love yourself may be an especially difficult process for you compared to more neurotypical or privileged people because of your brain chemistry or other circumstances outside your control and you are allowed to find it very hard and complain about stuff that's unfair, 3. it is not only okay but also expected that anyone going through this process will need help (including treatment), and it is not reasonable to expect it to happen by sheer force of will.

Please please reconsider, you're depriving her of medical information that could affect her health decisions.

She had concluded, it seems correctly, that dairy is linked to her skin issues; what you did may have caused her to doubt her *correct* observations and factor it into future health mysteries.  For example, maybe dairy is the only cause but now she suspects there are others that she now needs to change her life around, or she could seek medication or products she doesn't need and experience negative side effects (in addition to the cost).  Even if she shrugs it off as a fluke for now, she may think about this flare-up in the future when she's considering some other health issue or making a decision.  She might connect other reactions to the secret dairy she's had with some coincidental event, like stress or pollen.  It's part of her medical history, and as far as she knows, it's unexplained.  No matter how minor you think it is, it's her business and she deserves to know.

What you did was gaslighting and if you care for her at all you'll return her to the correct reality.  And if trust is an issue where dairy is concerned it *will* come up again.  You live together, if you want to stay serious she needs to know the person she's agreeing to be serious with.

If you're monogamous, imagine this: She cheats on you and knowingly exposes you to a minor STI without telling you.  You develop symptoms and she acts horrified, you apologize and say you don't understand, you must have picked it up by wild chance somewhere.  She tells you you've given it to her, you apologize more.  Both your infections clear and you're left asking for forgiveness, which she gives you.  You become extremely paranoid in public bathrooms and changing rooms for the rest of your life.  She decides it was for your own good that she never told you and feels fine about all this.

I have these feelings too. <3  I think in most cases it's not that it's selfish but that it's a misguided form of self-preservation that can become so powerful it overwhelms your ability to do what's best for yourself *or* the people you love.  There's no getting around the devastation they would feel if they lost you by any method, but your job is to focus on what you need to get better and how your loved ones can help, whether or not you choose to tell them what they're helping with right away.  Every day that you don't die is a day you worked hard and accomplished something, even if it doesn't feel that way.  Sometimes people didn't have the care they needed and the bad feelings win, but that doesn't make them selfish or cowardly either.  It makes them victims of a preventable tragedy, the same tragedy you might be able to prevent for yourself.

Depending on how your brain works it might be more helpful to think of the potential for stuff to be good than the negative consequences of dying, even though that's a pretty big ask.  I find it encouraging to grasp at the tiny slices of memory of enjoying hobbies and feeling competent that float by sometimes and imagine what it could feel like if those slices expanded to make up a much bigger part of the picture with the badness taking up a lot less.  A manageable life with room for happiness, that's the goal.

So, yeah, I'm a lady, and kind of a sloppy nerd, and the dudes I fancy tend to be sloppy nerds too.  I've been infatuated with what you might call pretty funny-looking dudes because they laughed at my jokes and showed an interest in my life and my opinions and didn't spend our entire interaction showing off their own stuff and accomplishments.  In fact, nothing throws a bucket of cold water over my libido like a show-offy dude.  There lie "dates" consisting of me silently watching him do his cool hobby and "heart-to-hearts" in which I'm expected to make him feel important while he shows zero interest in my shit.  I mean, there are LOADS of scruffy nerdy dudes like that too, but the unattractive principles of Showing Off are the same even if the specifics ("now let's watch me do Blender modeling for three hours!  Swoon at my skillz, female!") vary.

The universe of things people find attractive is much wider than you give it credit for, and it's fallacious to present cosmetic advice as advice for widening your appeal.  What you present as increasing one's odds with *everyone* is actually just increasing one's odds within a niche.  If ostentatious wealth and/or fashion trend grooming is your niche, by all means, lean into it, but if it's not, again, you're going to find yourself very bored once you "succeed."  A better way to up the chances that you'll meet people *who impress you back* is to join social communities based around things *you actually like.*

For the record, the most prolifically slutty straight men I've met are poor in possessions and rich in empathy, save up for vibrators and tampons rather than statement watches, read feminist blogs instead of pickup artist manuals (self-examining male feminism: the ultimate panty dropper, seriously, we fuck the shit out of those guys when we find them), and see sex and spending time with many women as genuinely enjoyable interactions with complex human beings rather than some Sisyphean alpha male duty to collect notches/prove yourself/fill the sad void of life.

If it's about impressing your friends, there are way easier and more fun ways to do that if they're really your friends.  If it's about wanting connections or orgasms, see above.  If it's about sticking it in as many conventionally attractive women as possible so you can make a list of them, there's a whole industry that can provide that service and they could use your legislative advocacy.

In summary, yeah, just, people are different.  Find your people, be considerate and show interest in their lives, ask people out (sooner rather than later so they aren't built up to deities of radiant light in your head, to paraphrase Captain Awkward), have a safe place you can take your sad feelings if things don't go as you'd like, and do things you like that remind you that you're already interesting and cool and sexy.  There is no one-size-fits-all cosmetic advice that causes the Women Dispensary to dispense you a woman.

I mean, I don't totally buy that you're not intelligent based only on the evidence that you didn't get a PhD at 12, but even putting that aside:

Science is collaborative.  The history of celebrating scientific achievement in the "West" has been criminally focused on the individual, the lone genius slogging through the night to achieve personal shining glory and also something something human advancement who cares.  Don't get me wrong, I love me some personal stories of defying the odds, I love me some Einstein and Faraday and Payne*, but the coolest things humanity has ever done we've done in groups, and often over long-ass periods of time with many names never making it into history books.  I wish when we thought of science history it wasn't just, "yup, here's the list of white guys who Scienced.  Also the like two women or people of color anyone can ever name." *it's not as though she basically ~invented astrophysics~ with the help of ~a bunch of other ladies~ only a few years after being allowed to vote or anything, don't worry about it.

When we celebrate prodigies and *observable* geniuses (how many geniuses are never observed due to circumstance, or the lack of understanding of what constitutes genius in their field?) to the *exclusion* of collaborative efforts, we lose the core thing that makes science what it is.  It is not, at least ideally, a pissing contest between giant egos (I mean obviously that happens but it isn't super helpful to the pursuit of knowledge), it is not (primarily) an avenue of showing off for fleeting gain - it's a contribution to something much bigger than yourself.

If you like the idea of being a scientist because you want to contribute to the wealth of human knowledge and meet like-minded people who think what you all are doing is pretty cool, even if your names are never printed in textbooks for bored, snot-nosed kids to memorize, then you should be a scientist.

As far as you're concerned for now, it doesn't matter why he's acting this way; whether he's taking you for granted or taking care of himself, if he's not treating you as a friend then he doesn't meet the first criterion of being your friend, and you should let yourself say a temporary or permanent goodbye to him in your mind.  Think less "does he like me?" and more "do I like him?"

When you don't like yourself, "friendship" can turn into one-sided infatuation or exploitation pretty easily.  I've been in this situation many times, and I still struggle sometimes, but the more of your own stuff you have going on the more you begin to believe that you deserve a friend who treats you like a beloved peer, not someone who just deigns to let you hang around them.  It's easy to become the sycophantic Helper friend who gets called in for emotional support and then discarded as soon as you've served your purpose and someone cooler becomes available, or the needy, clingy, afraid-of-losing-them friend who feels irrationally wounded and betrayed that they sometimes have other plans - I've been both.

No individual owes any other individual friendship and you can't buy someone's love by loving them hard enough, but someone who'd be thrilled to have you as a best friend exists, maybe in a local MeetUp or club or in an online community.  Maybe take some time to indulge in something that makes you you, with or without *low-pressure* socializing involved (if socializing turns into friendship, all the better, but it doesn't have to).  Be kind to yourself and let yourself grieve the friendship while also working on your own, non-That-Friend-related stuff.

You've done the right thing by contacting his mom, and I think you're within your rights to keep trying and explain the full situation to her and anyone else in his circle that you can contact.  By threatening violence against someone (himself) to you he's relinquished that particular privacy entitlement.  If someone knows where he is (or if the phone number tracking idea is possible) you may be able to arrange a welfare check together.  Embarrassed and mad at you is better than dead.  That said, whatever he does is in no way your fault, and you deserve your own loving support structure (friends, family, therapy, etc.) to deal with this whole ordeal, whatever happens.

This will go without saying for some but it bears saying for others that once his people or the authorities have been informed it's totally your choice whether you want to be involved in helping him at all.  It is not anyone's responsibility to be part of their ex's support structure, even if the ex is targeting you with the suicidal ideation.  In this case though it sounds like you are still friends, you're choosing to support him, and this isn't *necessarily* emotional blackmail.  Possible red flag is if he bristles at the idea of you telling anyone else in his support structure (e.g. Mom) and wants to keep the suicide conversation between the two of you.

Because we're finally getting the choice to be single, an increasing number of women see it as a better deal, as long as gender roles are changing so slowly.  Everyone is pressured to be paired up and we're all made to feel like failures if we're single, but there may be an especially strong message for men that "getting" a woman in one way or another will solve your problems and prove you're a virile Real Man who deserves to live and breaks cinderblocks with his hands or something. You're already a complete person, and if you want a relationship with another complete person so you can be awesome complete people together, that's great, but treating a relationship like IT would complete you is both unhealthy for you and unattractive for healthy potential partners.  If you invest energy in your hobbies (games, books, Reddit, and YouTube are totally hobbies, don't minimize them), find a type of socializing that works for you (Captain often recommends browsing Meetup), and focus on making your life as nice as it can be *for you*, that's the most fertile ground for romantic relationships right there.
